tip: 'Tawar' = plain, unsweetened (and also 'to bargain'): 'teh tawar' = unsweetened tea.
'HP' (say ha-pe) is the everyday word for phone; 'ponsel' sounds formal. 'Mengecek HP' = check the phone.
Setting an alarm is 'memasang' (root 'pasang') or 'setel': 'pasang alarm jam lima' = set a 5 a.m. alarm.
'Boleh minta' + the thing is the all-purpose polite request – no 'may I have' verb chain needed: 'boleh minta password wifi-nya'.
'Ngecas' puts the casual 'nge-' prefix on the borrowed root 'cas' (from 'charge'): loanwords take Indonesian prefixes freely.
'Numpang' = politely use someone's facility: 'numpang ngecas' = charge here, if I may.
Even a borrowed root takes the passive 'di-': 'cas' (charge) becomes 'dicas' = gets charged. 'HP saya dicas' = my phone was charged – no 'was' word needed.
'Tinggal' usually means 'live, stay', but before an amount it means what's left: 'tinggal sepuluh persen' = only ten percent remaining. Context picks the meaning.
'Mengunduh' = download; in speech people also just say 'download': 'download aplikasinya'.
'Diskon' is the everyday word; 'potongan harga' is what a sale poster says.
'Pengeluaran' comes from 'keluar' (go out): expenses are literally the going-out of money. Its mirror is 'pemasukan' (income), from 'masuk' (come in).
'Absen' in Indonesia = to mark attendance (clock in), not to be absent.
'Ojol' is short for 'ojek online', the app-booked motorbike taxi.
'Ter-' for accidents: 'tersesat' = to get lost (not on purpose), from 'sesat'.
Doubling turns a one-off into an on-and-off: 'putus' = cut off, 'putus-putus' = keeps cutting out. 'Sering putus-putus' (often cutting out) is the classic bad-connection complaint.
English loans work as verbs with nothing added: 'kami video call' – no 'melakukan', no verb ending. Same with 'meeting', 'chat', and 'upload' in office talk.
'Mematikan' is literally 'make dead': 'mati' (dead) + 'me-...-kan'. Turning off the 'mikrofon' means killing it – the same logic as English 'kill the lights'.
'Ter-' + 'simpan' = a state, not an action: 'tersimpan' = (safely) stored, with no one doing the storing.
'RT' ('rukun tetangga') = your neighborhood block; nearly every 'RT' has its own 'grup'.
'Gambar selamat pagi' – flowery good-morning images – are a daily ritual in Indonesian family chat groups, sent most faithfully by 'om dan tante'.
'Belum tentu' is literally 'not yet certain': 'belum tentu benar' = not necessarily true. Indonesian often uses 'belum' (not yet) where English says a flat 'not'.
Passive 'di-' + agent, no 'oleh' needed: 'dikirim adik saya' = sent by my little sister.
Object first + 'saya kirim' = everyday passive: 'lokasi restorannya saya kirim' = I'll send the restaurant's location.
'Kampung halaman' is a fixed pair meaning your family's hometown – where you're from, not just any village. Plain 'kampung' can be any village or neighborhood.
'Password' is the everyday word; 'kata sandi' is what formal screens call it.
'Mengunggah' = upload and 'mengunduh' = download are near-twins that are easy to swap. Casual speech dodges the problem: people say 'upload' and 'download' as-is.
'Dari Sabang sampai Merauke' = 'all across Indonesia' – Sabang is the far western tip, Merauke the far eastern one. The set phrase for the whole nation.
The 'me-' prefix can turn a noun into a verb: 'laut' (sea) becomes 'melaut', to head out to sea – which is what 'nelayan' (fishermen) do every morning.
Rice has three names: 'padi' in the field, 'beras' raw in the bag, 'nasi' cooked on your plate.
'Ber-' can mean 'having': 'gunung berapi' is literally a mountain having 'api' (fire) – a volcano. The fire is built right into the word.
